o: We are given a valid IPv4 address string containing exactly three '.' characters, and we must return a new string where each '.' is replaced by the four-character sequence '[.]'. For example, "1.1.1.1" becomes "1[.]1[.]1[.]1" because each of the three dots is swapped for '[.]'. In "255.100.50.0", the three separators between the octets become '[.]' while the digits stay untouched. Since the input is guaranteed valid, we never need to validate the format — this is purely a string transformation problem. The output length is fixed: input length plus 9 (three dots each growing from 1 to 4 characters), so any linear scan suffices.
k: The transformation is a simple character-by-character substitution: copy every character, but emit '[.]' whenever a '.' appears.
Because the input is guaranteed valid, no parsing or validation is needed — just a single pass over the string.
Building with a mutable buffer (StringBuilder / list / string stream) avoids quadratic repeated concatenation in languages with immutable strings.

a.i: Walk through the input once and build the result into a growable buffer. Every non-dot character is appended as-is; a dot triggers appending the literal '[.]'. This directly mirrors the definition of defanging and works in one pass.
s: Iterate over each character c of the input address.
If c == '.', append '[.]' to the buffer; otherwise append c.
Return the buffer converted to a string.
a.t: O(n) — each character of the input is visited exactly once.
a.sp: O(n) — the output string has length n + 9; auxiliary space beyond the output is O(1).

a.i: Every standard library offers a way to replace all occurrences of a substring or split on a delimiter. Replacing "." with "[.]" (or splitting on "." and joining with "[.]") accomplishes the task in one line, delegating the loop to optimized library code.
s: Call the language's replace-all function on the input with pattern "." and replacement "[.]".
a.t: O(n) — the replacement scans the string once (C++ in-place replace keeps total work linear since there are only three dots).
a.sp: O(n) — a new string of length n + 9 is produced (C++ modifies in place but still conceptually O(n) output).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 to show you understand the mechanics, then mention that a built-in replace (Approach 2) is what you'd write in production code. Common pitfalls: using naive string concatenation in a loop in Java/Python can degrade performance (though negligible at n ≈ 15); forgetting to advance the search position after an in-place C++ replace causes infinite loops; and in JavaScript, `replace` without a regex only replaces the first occurrence, so use split/join or a global regex `/\./g`. Edge cases are minimal since the input is guaranteed valid — exactly three dots, digits only. Likely follow-ups: generalize to IPv6 (same idea, different separator), handle invalid inputs (add validation), or do it in-place with minimal extra memory.
